My great-grandmother always advised me to prep an escape route and travel goods if you live in an urban area. She saw cities become death traps during the great depression and it will be much worse if a war shows up at your door.

1) No cars. Plan to use a bike or walk. If you are in urban area you must assume that every major road way will be congested in a major exodus.

2) Have maps and compasses and make a habit of scouting areas that may be safe to take refuge and lesser traveled roads, now. You should know how to escape your city without using a single major roadway.

3) It may be more practical to only carry water and forage for food on the way. I was also taught to carry a jar and some tubbing to distill small amounts of water on the go.

4) Carry a bebe gun to hunt. Cities are filled with squirrels and pigeons.

There are only two options to really consider here:

  1. Evacuating, or

Flash charging technology to charge Geneva e-buses in 15 seconds

Look like whoever wrote the article didn't read it : It charge at normal power for the first 15 seconds then add 600kW for the next five minutes.

Must double up as a space heater too...

First up, it takes 15 seconds to start, it doesn't finish in 15 seconds. Even at the 600kW charging rate mentioned, 15 seconds would get you 9,000kJ of charge, or only 2.5kWh. For reference, a Tesla Model S has an 80-90kWh battery. A bus would have a much, much larger battery than that.

Secondly, 600kW is a lot. Like, a lot a lot. Even if the charger is supplying 600V (about the max for DC systems before you start having to use some serious, and heavy, equipment for circuit breakers etc.) that's still 1000 Amps, which is huge. You lose 1% of your power as heat transferring 1000 Amps through 3m of 25mm copper cable.

That's a lot of juice (600kW) compared with what my car can handle (50kW DC) and it takes 20 mins for mine to reach 80% full. They're saying it will take 5 mins to charge the bus batteries at the terminus so we can figure that the bus must have a battery somewhere around 120 kWh.
